        <title type="text">Does Extended Resolution collapse to bounded extension depth?</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="sat" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="proof-complexity" />
        <author>
            <name>Jogenara</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/72711</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57294/does-extended-resolution-collapse-to-bounded-extension-depth" />
        <published>2026-10-15T05:22:47Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-15T07:30:32Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Extended Resolution (ER) allows extension variables to be introduced by definitions such as</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$y\leftrightarrow(a\land b)$</span></p>
<p>where <span class="math-container">$a$</span> and <span class="math-container">$b$</span> may be literals involving original variables or previously introduced extension variables.</p>
<p>Consider the following hierarchy of restricted ER proof systems. Every extension variable is defined using a fan-in-two Boolean gate, and the extension depth of a variable is the maximum number of extension gates on a dependency path from an original variable to that variable. Let <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_k$</span> be the system in which every extension variable has extension depth at most <span class="math-container">$k$</span>. The size of a proof includes the number of extension axioms, their encoding sizes, and all other proof lines.</p>
<p>Thus, <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_1$</span> permits extension variables defined directly from original variables, whereas <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_2$</span> also permits extension variables defined using variables of extension depth at most one, and so on. Ordinary ER is recovered when the allowed extension depth is not bounded by a fixed constant.</p>
<p>Question:</p>
<p>Does this hierarchy collapse at some fixed level under polynomial simulation? More precisely, is there a constant <span class="math-container">$k$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_k$</span> polynomially simulates unrestricted ER, or is there evidence that every fixed-depth restriction is strictly weaker than unrestricted ER?</p>
<p>A related question is whether there are known proof-complexity techniques that could establish separations between <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_k$</span> and <span class="math-container">$\mathrm{ER}_{k+1}$</span>, or show that these systems are polynomially equivalent.</p>
<p>I am particularly interested in known results on restricted extension variables, bounded-depth extension definitions, and the relationship between extension depth and proof size.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="ds.algorithms" />

        <author>

        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57293/feedback-on-a-sorting-algorithm" />
        <published>2026-10-14T23:18:04Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-14T23:18:04Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am trying to analyze a sorting algorithm that uses an alternating sorting pattern across three piles (Pile A, Pile B, Pile C). I want to see how this pre-sorting rule affects the balance and solvability of a partition problem.</p>
<p>The Algorithm Step-by-Step:
Let S be a collection of 3N items with positive integer weights.</p>
<ol>
<li><p>The Pre-Sorting Sieve:
For each step i from 1 to N, take the next 3 items from S and sort them by weight: Large, Medium, and Small.</p>
<ul>
<li>If i is even: Add Large to Pile_A, Small to Pile_B, and Medium to Pile_C.</li>
<li>If i is odd: Add Small to Pile_A, Large to Pile_B, and Medium to Pile_C.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><p>The Partition Search:
After all items are sorted, we look for an exact matching partition. We want to find a way to split the Medium items in Pile_C into two sub-piles, C_to_A and C_to_B, such that:</p>
<ul>
<li>Every single element of Pile_C is placed exactly once into either C_to_A or C_to_B.</li>
<li>The Target Equation: Sum(Pile_A) + Sum(C_to_A) == Sum(Pile_B) + Sum(C_to_B)
If a matching split is found, the program outputs &quot;yes&quot; and halts.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p>My Questions for the Board:</p>
<ol>
<li><p>Imbalance Bounds: Because the algorithm alternates assigning Large and Small items between Pile A and Pile B, the initial difference between their sums, |Sum(Pile_A) - Sum(Pile_B)|, stays highly constrained. If the initial item weights are randomly chosen from a uniform distribution, how do we write a formula for the expected variance of this difference as N grows?</p>
</li>
<li><p>Phase Transition and Density: While it is easy to construct worst-case inputs where a perfect partition is completely impossible, what happens under typical conditions? Since Pile C accumulates N median elements (a linear capacity of O(N)) while the initial imbalance between A and B is tightly bound, does this system undergo a sharp statistical phase transition where a valid partition becomes almost certain for dense, random inputs as N approaches infinity?</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>I would love to see any formulas, recursive relationships, or references to similar 3-pile sorting partition problems! Thanks for any help.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

            <p>I’m currently finishing my undergraduate degree in CS and preparing to start my Masters. I am very passionate about TCS and my primary goal has always been to stay in academia and build a long-term research career in pure theory.</p>

At the same time, it feels like the entire academic landscape, from university funding to faculty hiring, is aggressively pivoting toward ML.</p>
<p>I’d love to hear honest perspectives from current PhD students, post-docs, and professors in TCS :</p>
<p>Do you foresee AI fundamentally changing or even automating the core work of theoretical computer scientists in the coming decade?</p>
<p>Are you feeling a squeeze in funding, grants, and tenure-track positions for pure theory because of the AI boom?</p>
<p>For someone just starting their graduate journey, is it still a wise decision to go &quot;all in&quot; on traditional TCS? Or is it becoming essential to pivot and find an intersection between theory and AI to survive in modern academia?</p>
<p>I really want to follow my passion for foundational theory, but I also want to be realistic about the academic ecosystem I’ll be operating in 5-10 years from now. Any advice or insights would be greatly appreciated!</p>

        <title type="text">Is NP-completeness known for quadratic selection over 3-element chains with matching interactions?</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="cc.complexity-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="reference-request" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="np-hardness" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="optimization" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="quadratic" />
        <author>
            <name>Sebastien</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/81128</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57284/is-np-completeness-known-for-quadratic-selection-over-3-element-chains-with-matc" />
        <published>2026-10-09T23:24:30Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-09T23:31:44Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am looking for a bibliographic reference concerning a restricted precedence-constrained quadratic selection problem.</p>
<h3>1. Problem definition</h3>
<p>Let <span class="math-container">$P=(V,\leq)$</span> be a finite, explicitly represented poset. Given integer profits <span class="math-container">$p_v$</span>, quadratic coefficients <span class="math-container">$q_{uv}$</span>, a cardinality bound <span class="math-container">$L$</span>, and a threshold <span class="math-container">$\Theta$</span>, consider the following decision problem.</p>
<p>Does there exist a downward-closed subset <span class="math-container">$S\subseteq V$</span> satisfying</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|S|\leq L
$$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
f(S)=\sum_{v\in S}p_v+
\sum_{\{u,v\}\subseteq S}q_{uv}
\geq\Theta?
$$</span></p>
<p>Every unordered pair is counted exactly once. All integer data are explicitly encoded in binary.</p>
<h3>2. Simultaneous structural restrictions</h3>
<p>I am interested in the case where all five restrictions hold simultaneously:</p>
<ol>
<li>The poset is a disjoint union of chains of <strong>exactly three elements</strong>.</li>
<li>The graph of nonzero quadratic interactions is a <strong>matching</strong>.</li>
<li>Every nonzero interaction joins <strong>incomparable elements</strong>.</li>
<li>Every linear profit satisfies <span class="math-container">$p_v\in\{0,1\}$</span>.</li>
<li>Every quadratic coefficient satisfies <span class="math-container">$q_{uv}\in\{0,-1\}$</span>.</li>
</ol>
<h3>3. Candidate NP-completeness reduction</h3>
<p>Consider a reduction from <strong>Independent Set on graphs of maximum degree three</strong>.</p>
<p>Given a simple graph <span class="math-container">$G=(U,E)$</span> and an integer <span class="math-container">$k$</span>, construct a chain</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
a_{v,1}&lt;a_{v,2}&lt;a_{v,3}
$$</span></p>
<p>for every vertex <span class="math-container">$v\in U$</span>.</p>
<p>There are no precedence relations between distinct chains.</p>
<p>Assign linear profits as follows:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
p_{a_{v,1}}=p_{a_{v,2}}=0,
\qquad
p_{a_{v,3}}=1.
$$</span></p>
<p>Since every vertex has degree at most three, assign its incident edges injectively to the three positions of its chain.</p>
<p>For each edge <span class="math-container">$uv\in E$</span>, introduce exactly one quadratic interaction of coefficient <span class="math-container">$-1$</span> between the two positions assigned to that edge at <span class="math-container">$u$</span> and <span class="math-container">$v$</span>.</p>
<p>All other quadratic coefficients are zero.</p>
<p>Set</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
L=3k,\qquad \Theta=k.
$$</span></p>
<p>The construction is polynomial and satisfies all five restrictions simultaneously.</p>
<h3>4. Normalization argument</h3>
<p>Every ideal intersects each chain in a prefix.</p>
<p>On the constructed instances, any selected proper prefix can be removed without decreasing the objective:</p>
<ul>
<li>It contains no terminal element and therefore contributes zero linear profit.</li>
<li>Removing it eliminates only nonpositive quadratic interactions.</li>
<li>Removing it preserves downward closure and cannot violate the cardinality bound.</li>
</ul>
<p>Repeating this operation yields an ideal consisting entirely of complete chains or absent chains.</p>
<p>This normalization claim concerns the constructed instances, not arbitrary instances satisfying the five restrictions.</p>
<p>Let <span class="math-container">$T\subseteq U$</span> denote the vertices whose chains are completely selected.</p>
<p>Then</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|S|=3|T|
$$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
f(S)=|T|-|E(T)|,
$$</span></p>
<p>where <span class="math-container">$E(T)$</span> denotes the set of edges induced by <span class="math-container">$T$</span>.</p>
<h3>5. Equivalence</h3>
<p><strong>Forward direction.</strong></p>
<p>If <span class="math-container">$G$</span> has an independent set of size at least <span class="math-container">$k$</span>, select exactly <span class="math-container">$k$</span> corresponding complete chains.</p>
<p>Then</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|S|=3k\leq L
$$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
f(S)=k\geq\Theta.
$$</span></p>
<p><strong>Reverse direction.</strong></p>
<p>Suppose a feasible ideal exists with</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|S|\leq3k
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f(S)\geq k.
$$</span></p>
<p>Normalize it as above.</p>
<p>The corresponding vertex subset <span class="math-container">$T$</span> satisfies</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|T|\leq k
$$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|T|-|E(T)|\geq k.
$$</span></p>
<p>Since <span class="math-container">$|E(T)|\geq0$</span>, these inequalities imply</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
|T|=k
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|E(T)|=0.
$$</span></p>
<p>Therefore, <span class="math-container">$T$</span> is an independent set of size <span class="math-container">$k$</span>.</p>
<p>Membership in NP follows from polynomial-time verification of downward closure, cardinality, and the objective value.</p>
<p>Thus the reduction appears to establish NP-completeness under all five restrictions.</p>
<h3>6. Bibliographic question</h3>
<p><strong>Is the NP-completeness of this exact restricted problem already established in the literature, either explicitly or as an immediate consequence of a more general theorem?</strong></p>
<p>I am particularly interested in relevant results concerning:</p>
<ul>
<li>Precedence-constrained quadratic knapsack problems.</li>
<li>Quadratic optimization over order ideals.</li>
<li>Closure problems involving pairwise penalties.</li>
<li>Complexity results under simultaneous structural restrictions.</li>
</ul>
<p>The general quadratic selection model and related penalty-based formulations have existing precedents.</p>
<p><strong>I make no claim of novelty for the general formulation or the reduction technique.</strong> My question concerns whether the exact combination of restrictions above is already covered by a known result.</p>
<p>A precise reference or a short derivation from an established theorem would be greatly appreciated.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <published>2026-10-08T23:51:45Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-11T10:27:32Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Note: I posted this on cs stack exchange first (<a href="https://cs.stackexchange.com/questions/176677/efficient-methods-for-finding-origami-crease-patterns">here</a>) and one of the comments suggested it would be a better fit for this exchange; and I also believe that it's more fit asked on this exchange website.<br><br> Since Robert Lang, there has been a problem in computation: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_paper_folding" rel="nofollow noreferrer">finding efficient origami/geometrical folding algorithms</a></p>
<p>See this example:</p>
<p><a href="https://i.sstatic.net/QSLotwin.png" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/QSLotwin.png" alt="Folding a rabbit" /></a></p>
<p>Where the 3D desired pattern is given and the algorithm solve for where the paper needs to be creased and folded in order to achieve the shape.</p>
<p>An efficient algorithm in this context is one with the least number of folds.  And this is NP-complete.</p>
<p>There have been outstanding improvement in computational origami with the works of prof. Erik Demaine and prof. Tomohiro Tachi their respective colleague (mainly at MIT and Tokyo University); Having proved a relatively efficient algorithm that solve these problems, especially with a software developed by Tachi in 2008 (<a href="https://origami.c.u-tokyo.ac.jp/%7Etachi/software/" rel="nofollow noreferrer">see here</a>).</p>
<p>Regarding this I have a question:</p>
<p><strong>What were the main improvements on this topic since?</strong>
As far as I could find there were no efforts on this after 2017 (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_paper_folding#Research" rel="nofollow noreferrer">again see here</a>) which they were able to find &quot;practical methods&quot; of finding folding patterns; But after watching lectures on MIT OCW by prof. Erik D. for example <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-849-geometric-folding-algorithms-linkages-origami-polyhedra-fall-2012/" rel="nofollow noreferrer">this</a>, where he said that the work done in 2017 was mostly revisionary rather than adding any more substantial work. <br><a href="https://erikdemaine.org/papers/OSME2001/paper.pdf" rel="nofollow noreferrer">another paper, released in 2001 by Erik D. and Robert L.</a> discussing and proving important material.</p>
<h2>Saving paper</h2>
<p>Also there have been attempts by approximately the same handful of people (as this area is not really in the limelight of any field) to prove efficient algorithms for finding a folding that uses the least amount of paper.</p>
<p>Because of course when the sheet or paper is folded the fold itself will create unused paper.</p>
<p>I haven't actually given it much thought but I assume that it's also NP-complete?</p>
<p>I couldn't really find any recent improvements on this; and thus would really appreciate if someone knows about this(ese) yet very niche topic(s) and reaches out.
<br> Thanks in advance.</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">On AI Disclosure Statement Standards in TCS</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="soft-question" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="research-practice" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="ai.artificial-intel" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="ai-assissted-research" />
        <author>
            <name>Stefan G.</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/25284</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57278/on-ai-disclosure-statement-standards-in-tcs" />
        <published>2026-09-28T13:48:38Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-28T21:46:07Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p><strong>How should we evaluate AI disclosure statements, and what should they require?</strong></p>
<p>It seems readily apparent that many (most/all?) math/TCS paper in the future will require an AI Disclosure statement. Currently, there is no standard for what these statements contain, and what the language used even means.</p>
<p>Since we are in a major transition period, I think it would be expedient to introduce some clear AI Disclosure statement standards, so we can be scientifically honest about our research processes. Below are some suggestions, ranging in stringency.</p>
<p><strong>1. Open Source Everything:</strong> An detailed summary of how AI tools were engaged with, with every single prompt and output provided open source in a Git repo, with no modifications.</p>
<p><strong>2. Open Source with Editorial Power:</strong> Once again, a detailed summary of exactly how AI tools were used, and an open-sourcing of the prompts and outputs. Here, one would be allowed to use &quot;black-out&quot; on some prompts that the researcher felt were more personal, unrelated, or relating to follow-up/different research projects.</p>
<p><strong>3. Clear Distinctions of AI generated proofs:</strong> Here, prompts are not open source, but we develop a precise terminology on what it means for a proof or idea to be &quot;AI generated&quot;. A separate copy of the paper is posted which is annotated using this terminology.</p>
<p><strong>4. Soft Language:</strong> Usage of AI tools is admitted, and broadly the purposes of the tools are described. Some standards of language are agreed upon, but overall it is up to the researcher on how their interactions should be described.</p>
<p><strong>5. No Statements:</strong> We accept as a community that AI usage is common and okay, as long as everything is verified and well-presented. Authorship is redefined to be more of a communicatory role than an ownership role.</p>
<p>Currently, we are in the soft language category, and I would argue this is not desirable, at least until we have clear community standards as well as a scientific understanding of how to properly use these tools. We should also strive to have a clear idea of their many strengths, as well as their current weaknesses. It takes a community effort to achieve this, which is why I am proposing we adopt the standard of <strong>Open Source Everything</strong> for the foreseeable future.</p>
<p>What does everyone feel about these options, and how we should proceed?</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <author>
            <name>Kaveh</name>

        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57276/lean-libs-for-theoretical-computer-science" />
        <published>2026-09-27T23:38:44Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-30T22:17:40Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>It seems that using Lean+AI is becoming common in math research. I assume we will see similar trends in TCS and complexity theory.</p>
<p>What are the major libraries (or research programs) for formalizing TCS and complexity theory in Lean?</p>
<p>Essentially a library that has the concepts and results from textbooks (Sipser or Arora and Barak) and major interesting papers in it, maybe also the results mentioned in Completely Zoo.</p>
<p>Here is what I have found so far:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="http://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4" rel="nofollow noreferrer">MathLib</a> has some very basic concepts.</li>
<li><a href="http://github.com/leanprover/cslib" rel="nofollow noreferrer">cslib</a> seems to be the main lib for cs and has more, but still far from containing basic textbook results.</li>
</ul>
<p>And a few more that I have not check but suggested by Claude:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Computability/Complexity.lean" rel="nofollow noreferrer">formal-conjectures</a></strong> (Google DeepMind). P, NP, and coNP defined on Mathlib's polynomial-time notion, with P versus NP stated as a conjecture.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib" rel="nofollow noreferrer">complexitylib</a></strong> (Samuel Schlesinger). Arora–Barak-style multi-tape machines. Claims Cook–Levin, time hierarchy, Savitch, Sipser–Lautemann, Cobham, circuit results, and PCP, all sorry-free.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/DominicBreuker/cook-levin-lean" rel="nofollow noreferrer">cook-levin-lean</a></strong> (Dominic Breuker).</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity" rel="nofollow noreferrer">descriptive-complexity</a></strong> (Senellart and Gnatenko, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18261" rel="nofollow noreferrer">arXiv 2609.18261</a>, September 2026). Machine-free Cook–Levin via first-order reductions, all 21 Karp problems, NL = coNL, with bridges to machine definitions.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/formalcs/circuit-complexity" rel="nofollow noreferrer">circuit-complexity</a></strong> (formalcs, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24188" rel="nofollow noreferrer">arXiv 2609.24188</a>, September 2026). Boolean circuits, the switching lemma, PARITY ∉ AC⁰, Razborov–Smolensky.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/DominikPeters/HardnessReductionsLean" rel="nofollow noreferrer">HardnessReductionsLean</a></strong> (Dominik Peters). Sixty NP-hardness reductions in a cost-annotated combinator language, no machine model.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong><a href="https://github.com/EdouardBonnet/classical-complexity" rel="nofollow noreferrer">classical-complexity</a></strong> (Édouard Bonnet). Space classes L, NL, PSPACE, NPSPACE on a read-only-input machine. Reuses a P that shares formal-conjectures' definition.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Is there a Lean lib for TCS and complexity theory that people are using in their research? Is there any other major project to create a Lean lib for TCS and complexity theory other than those listed above?</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Can Boolean Nullstellensatz dual witnesses be represented by few Boolean evaluations?</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="sat" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="boolean-functions" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="coding-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="proof-complexity" />
        <author>
            <name>z.10.46</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/74234</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57272/can-boolean-nullstellensatz-dual-witnesses-be-represented-by-few-boolean-evaluat" />
        <published>2026-09-19T23:12:21Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-19T23:12:21Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am studying degree lower bounds for Nullstellensatz type refutations of unsatisfiable <span class="math-container">$3$</span> CNF formulas over <span class="math-container">$GF(2)$</span> in the Boolean quotient ring.</p>
<p>Let</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\Phi=C_1\land\cdots\land C_m$</span></p>
<p>be a <span class="math-container">$3$</span> CNF formula on Boolean variables <span class="math-container">$x_1,\ldots,x_n$</span>, with the Boolean relations</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$x_i^2=x_i$</span>.</p>
<p>For each clause <span class="math-container">$C_i$</span>, let <span class="math-container">$f_i$</span> be its falsifying indicator polynomial. For example,</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$C=(x_1\lor\neg x_2\lor x_3)$</span></p>
<p>is represented by</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$f_C=(1+x_1)x_2(1+x_3)$</span>.</p>
<p>Thus <span class="math-container">$\Phi$</span> is satisfiable exactly when</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$f_1=\cdots=f_m=0$</span></p>
<p>has a Boolean solution.</p>
<p>For an unsatisfiable formula, I consider a Nullstellensatz type refutation</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(x)f_i(x)=1$</span></p>
<p>in</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$R=GF(2)[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_1^2-x_1,\ldots,x_n^2-x_n)$</span>.</p>
<p>I define</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$d^*(F)=\min{d:\exists h_1,\ldots,h_m,\ \sum_i h_if_i=1,\ \deg(\operatorname{ml}(h_if_i))\le d}$</span>,</p>
<p>where <span class="math-container">$\operatorname{ml}$</span> denotes the multilinear representative in the Boolean quotient.</p>
<p>For a fixed degree <span class="math-container">$d$</span>, I form the linear system</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$M_dc=e_0$</span></p>
<p>over <span class="math-container">$GF(2)$</span>, where the rows are indexed by the multilinear monomials <span class="math-container">$x_S$</span> with <span class="math-container">$|S|\le d$</span>, and the columns are the coefficient vectors of all admissible polynomials <span class="math-container">$\operatorname{ml}(x_Tf_i)$</span> satisfying</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\deg(\operatorname{ml}(x_Tf_i))\le d$</span>.</p>
<p>Here <span class="math-container">$e_0$</span> is the coefficient vector of the constant polynomial <span class="math-container">$1$</span>.</p>
<h3>The dual witness</h3>
<p>If this system is inconsistent, linear duality gives a vector</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$y=(y_S)_{|S|\le d}$</span></p>
<p>such that</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$y_\varnothing=1$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\sum_{S:,|S|\le d} y_S [x_S]\operatorname{ml}(x_Tf_i)=0$</span></p>
<p>for every <span class="math-container">$i$</span> and every monomial <span class="math-container">$x_T$</span> such that</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\deg(\operatorname{ml}(x_Tf_i))\le d$</span>,</p>
<p>where <span class="math-container">$[x_S]p$</span> denotes the coefficient of the multilinear monomial <span class="math-container">$x_S$</span> in <span class="math-container">$p$</span>.</p>
<p>Equivalently, define the linear functional</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$L_y(\sum_{|S|\le d} a_Sx_S)=\sum_{|S|\le d} a_Sy_S$</span>.</p>
<p>Then</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$L_y(1)=1$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$L_y(\operatorname{ml}(x_Tf_i))=0$</span></p>
<p>for every admissible <span class="math-container">$i,T$</span>.</p>
<p>Thus a degree lower bound can be expressed through the existence of a degree-<span class="math-container">$d$</span> linear functional annihilating all admissible clause multiples while satisfying <span class="math-container">$L_y(1)=1$</span>.</p>
<h3>A restricted representation of the dual witness</h3>
<p>I am interested in the following particular representation of such a witness:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$y_S=\sum_{r=1}^R\prod_{j\in S}a_{rj},\qquad a_{rj}\in GF(2)$</span>.</p>
<p>If</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$a^{(r)}=(a_{r1},\ldots,a_{rn})\in{0,1}^n$</span>,</p>
<p>then this is equivalent to</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$L_y(p)=\sum_{r=1}^R p(a^{(r)})$</span></p>
<p>for every multilinear polynomial <span class="math-container">$p$</span> of degree at most <span class="math-container">$d$</span>.</p>
<p>Indeed, for a multilinear monomial <span class="math-container">$x_S$</span>,</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$x_S(a^{(r)})=\prod_{j\in S}a_{rj}$</span>.</p>
<p>Thus <span class="math-container">$y$</span> is represented as a sum, over <span class="math-container">$GF(2)$</span>, of <span class="math-container">$R$</span> Boolean evaluation functionals.</p>
<p>For <span class="math-container">$R=1$</span>, <span class="math-container">$L_y$</span> is evaluation at a single Boolean assignment. For larger <span class="math-container">$R$</span>, cancellations modulo <span class="math-container">$2$</span> between different assignments are possible.</p>
<p>Since the coefficients are in <span class="math-container">$GF(2)$</span>, repeated evaluation points cancel in pairs. Hence one may equivalently restrict to distinct Boolean assignments with odd multiplicity.</p>
<p>I am not claiming that every dual witness has such a representation with small <span class="math-container">$R$</span>. I am asking whether this representation, or the corresponding minimum value of <span class="math-container">$R$</span>, is already known under another name.</p>
<p>For a given dual witness <span class="math-container">$y$</span>, let <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> denote the minimum integer <span class="math-container">$R$</span> such that</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$y_S=\sum_{r=1}^R\prod_{j\in S}a_{rj}$</span></p>
<p>for every <span class="math-container">$S$</span> with <span class="math-container">$|S|\le d$</span>, where <span class="math-container">$a_{rj}\in GF(2)$</span>.</p>
<p>In small computational experiments, I found unsatisfiable formulas for which <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> appeared substantially smaller than the dimension of the ambient degree-<span class="math-container">$d$</span> dual space.</p>
<p>For example, for one instance with <span class="math-container">$n=8$</span> and <span class="math-container">$d^*(F)=5$</span>, the ambient dual space of multilinear polynomials of degree at most <span class="math-container">$4$</span> has dimension</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$N(8,4)=\sum_{k=0}^4\binom{8}{k}=163$</span>,</p>
<p>whereas I found a degree-<span class="math-container">$4$</span> dual witness representable using only a few dozen Boolean evaluations.</p>
<p>These are only computational observations, not an asymptotic claim.</p>
<h3>Questions</h3>
<ol>
<li>Has the representation</li>
</ol>
<p><span class="math-container">$y_S=\sum_{r=1}^R\prod_{j\in S}a_{rj}$</span></p>
<p>been studied previously in proof complexity, algebraic complexity, coding theory, Boolean Fourier analysis, or the theory of moment matrices?</p>
<ol start="2">
<li><p>Given a dual witness <span class="math-container">$y$</span>, is there a known characterization or upper bound for the minimum <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> for which such a representation exists?</p>
</li>
<li><p>Is <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> related to a standard complexity or rank parameter, such as tensor rank, symmetric tensor rank, binary tensor rank, moment matrix rank, Fourier sparsity, or another notion of rank or sparsity over <span class="math-container">$GF(2)$</span>?</p>
</li>
<li><p>Can one construct explicit families of unsatisfiable <span class="math-container">$3$</span> CNF formulas <span class="math-container">$F_n$</span> for which</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p><span class="math-container">$d^*(F_n)=\Omega(n)$</span></p>
<p>while a degree-<span class="math-container">$d^*(F_n)-1$</span> dual witness has a representation with relatively small <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span>?</p>
<ol start="5">
<li>Conversely, are there known families for which every relevant degree-<span class="math-container">$d^*(F_n)-1$</span> dual witness requires <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> to be exponential or superpolynomial in <span class="math-container">$n$</span>?</li>
</ol>
<p>The distinction I am interested in is therefore between</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\text{the minimum Nullstellensatz degree }d^*(F)$</span></p>
<p>and</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$\text{the minimum number }R(y)\text{ of Boolean evaluations needed to represent a dual witness }y$</span>.</p>
<p>These may be different notions of complexity. In particular, even a polynomial bound on <span class="math-container">$R(y)$</span> would not immediately give a polynomial-time algorithm for <span class="math-container">$3$</span> SAT, since one would still need to find the corresponding Boolean assignments satisfying the dual constraints.</p>
<p>I would especially appreciate references connecting this representation with Nullstellensatz, Polynomial Calculus, Boolean moment methods, tensor decompositions, or low-rank representations of dual certificates.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Complexity of maintaining H-minor-freeness on edge insertions</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="reference-request" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-algorithms" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-minor" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="dynamic-algorithms" />
        <author>
            <name>Antoine Amarilli 'a3nm'</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/4795</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57269/complexity-of-maintaining-h-minor-freeness-on-edge-insertions" />
        <published>2026-09-18T11:31:17Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-19T16:53:46Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$H$</span> be a fixed graph (or a fixed finite family of graphs). I am curious about the worst-case complexity of the following problem: given an initially empty graph <span class="math-container">$G$</span>, insert vertices and edges into <span class="math-container">$G$</span> and maintain after every update the information of whether <span class="math-container">$G$</span> is <span class="math-container">$H$</span>-minor-free, i.e., detect the first edge addition that makes an <span class="math-container">$H$</span>-minor appear (or a minor from some graph in <span class="math-container">$H$</span>, if <span class="math-container">$H$</span> is a family). There are only insertions and no deletions. The complexity would be the worst-case complexity of every update, as a function of the current size of <span class="math-container">$G$</span> (independently from <span class="math-container">$H$</span>).</p>
<p><strong>In general, can we beat the bound obtained by re-computing H-minor-freeness at every step?</strong> This algorithm gives almost-linear time updates by <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03958" rel="nofollow noreferrer">this recent paper</a>, so can we get better than almost-linear time per update?</p>
<p>Some observations:</p>
<ul>
<li>When <span class="math-container">$H$</span> is a planar graph (or includes a planar graph), excluding <span class="math-container">$H$</span> implies that the treewidth must remain bounded; but I don't know what is the best bound on detecting that the treewidth of <span class="math-container">$G$</span> has exceeded a constant <span class="math-container">$k$</span>. <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01744" rel="nofollow noreferrer">This paper</a> looks relevant but is about maintaining a tree decomposition of a dynamic graph under a promise that the graph treewidth remains bounded, not about detecting when treewidth exceeds a threshold. That said Theorem 4.4 of <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03958" rel="nofollow noreferrer">this paper</a> suggests that we may be able to detect when the treewidth gets too large (and maintain a query output when the treewidth is bounded, so maintaining H-minor-freeness) in <span class="math-container">$O(n^{o(1)})$</span> per update. But this does not work for general <span class="math-container">$H$</span>.</li>
<li>When <span class="math-container">$H$</span> are precisely the forbidden minors <span class="math-container">$K_5$</span> and <span class="math-container">$K_{3,3}$</span> for planarity, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03449" rel="nofollow noreferrer">this paper</a> gives a polylogarithmic bound (also supporting edge deletions), but it is specific to this case</li>
</ul>

        </summary>

            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/78899</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57267/is-this-alternating-version-of-set-cover-np-complete" />
        <published>2026-09-17T05:36:23Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-19T21:49:11Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I have a problem that's similar to the set cover problem, and I want to know if it's NP-Complete. In the problem, we are given:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$
\begin{aligned}
&amp;U := \text{Universe set,} \\
&amp;X := \text{Subsets of U} \ \text{(Each set in X can be any size, but }|X| = O(c\log{|U|}))\text{,} \\
&amp;C := \text{Cover set} \ (\subseteq U)\text{,} \\
\end{aligned}
$</span></p>
<p>and a complete binary formula tree that's rooted in <span class="math-container">$\cup$</span> and alternates between the <span class="math-container">$\cup$</span> and <span class="math-container">$\cap$</span> operators. For example:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$
\begin{aligned}
&amp;\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \cup \\
&amp;\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \ \ \ \cap \quad \\
&amp;\quad \quad \cup \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \cup \quad \quad \quad \ \ \ \quad \cup \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \cup \\
&amp;\ \ \cap \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad  \cap \quad \quad \cap \quad \quad \cap \\
&amp;? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \quad ? \\
\end{aligned}
$</span></p>
<p>Tree size: <span class="math-container">$O(|U|^c)$</span>.</p>
<p><strong>Problem:</strong> Can you replace the question marks with sets from <span class="math-container">$X$</span> (repetition allowed) such that this formula computes exactly <span class="math-container">$C$</span>?</p>
<p><strong>Question:</strong> Is this problem NP-Complete under the <span class="math-container">$|X| = O(c\log{|U|})$</span> restriction?</p>
<p>If we allow <span class="math-container">$|X| = O(|U|^c)$</span>, then the problem is clearly NP-Complete since you can reduce from set cover. Simply set <span class="math-container">$C=U$</span>. If <span class="math-container">$k$</span> is the parameter in the set cover instance, create an alternating formula tree like above with depth <span class="math-container">$2\log_2{(k)}$</span>. Since we are trying to cover the whole universe, we can be greedy at the <span class="math-container">$\cap$</span> nodes and set <span class="math-container">$A \cap A = A$</span>. By simplifying the tree, we get <span class="math-container">$k-1$</span> union nodes left over where we have to find a cover of size <span class="math-container">$k$</span>.</p>
<p>But if it's going to be NP-Complete while restricting <span class="math-container">$|X|$</span> to be <span class="math-container">$O(c\log{|U|})$</span>, then somehow the intersection nodes have to be utilized and <span class="math-container">$C$</span> can't simply equal <span class="math-container">$U$</span>. If <span class="math-container">$|X|$</span> is restricted to <span class="math-container">$\log{(n)}$</span> in the classic set cover problem then you can clearly solve it in polynomial time. Simply use all of the sets in your cover, or try every combination. But here it's not so simple since there are the <span class="math-container">$\cap$</span> nodes and we are only trying to cover <span class="math-container">$C$</span>, not all of <span class="math-container">$U$</span>.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Complexity of determining if the edges of a directed graph can be partitioned into edge-disjoint simple cycles of length $>k$</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="cc.complexity-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-algorithms" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="np-hardness" />
        <author>
            <name>Antoine Amarilli 'a3nm'</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/4795</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57254/complexity-of-determining-if-the-edges-of-a-directed-graph-can-be-partitioned-in" />
        <published>2026-09-04T13:24:10Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-23T23:13:54Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>We are given a directed graph <span class="math-container">$G = (V, E)$</span> and we want to partition its edges into edge-disjoint subgraphs that are simple cycles, i.e., write <span class="math-container">$E = E_1 \uplus \cdots \uplus E_p$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$(V, E_i)$</span> for each <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i \leq p$</span> is precisely a simple cycle (plus isolated vertices), noting that &quot;cycles&quot; here also include graphs with only back-and-forth edges <span class="math-container">$(u,v)$</span> and <span class="math-container">$(v,u)$</span>, and graphs with only a self-loop <span class="math-container">$(u,u)$</span>.</p>
<p>Clearly <span class="math-container">$G$</span> can be assumed to be connected without loss of generality. It is not difficult to see that partitioning into edge-disjoint simple cycles can be done precisely when all vertices of <span class="math-container">$G$</span> have out-degree equal to their in-degree (i.e., when <span class="math-container">$G$</span> is Eulerian): that's clearly sufficient, and when it is true then we can compute a Eulerian trail and rewrite it iteratively to get a decomposition into simple cycles.</p>
<p>My question is: <strong>what if we want to partition <span class="math-container">$G$</span> into edge-disjoint simple cycles that must all have length greater than <span class="math-container">$k$</span> for some fixed <span class="math-container">$k$</span>?</strong> Of course it is still a necessary requirement that <span class="math-container">$G$</span> is Eulerian, but this is not sufficient. Clearly <span class="math-container">$k=1$</span> is easy (possible iff <span class="math-container">$G$</span> has no self-loop). However:</p>
<ul>
<li><span class="math-container">$k=2$</span> is unclear if <span class="math-container">$G$</span> contains bidirectional edges: we cannot eliminate such edges as their own 2-edge cycle, we may be able to decompose the graph in other ways but this does not seem straightforward</li>
<li><span class="math-container">$k=3$</span> is also unclear and seems related to the question of finding a <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0012365X9400183J" rel="nofollow noreferrer">triangle-free Eulerian tour</a> but it is not the same concept because in my question it is acceptable if the cycle decomposition does not come from a (connected) tour</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What is the complexity of this problem for various fixed values of <span class="math-container">$k$</span>?</strong> Can it be NP-complete?</p>
<p>The problem can also be posed on undirected graphs: there <span class="math-container">$k=1$</span> and <span class="math-container">$k=2$</span> make no sense, but <span class="math-container">$k=3$</span> and more make sense and I'm also not sure of the complexity.</p>
<p>Some related questions:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/39041/decomposition-of-edges-of-eulerian-graph-into-maximum-number-of-cycles">Partitioning the edges into the <strong>maximal number</strong> of simple cycles</a></li>
<li><a href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/46819/algorithm-for-finding-a-3-cycle-cover/46820#46820">Partitioning the <strong>vertices</strong> into vertex-disjoint cycles of length greater than <span class="math-container">$k$</span></a></li>
<li>Partitioning the edges into vertex-disjoint cycles of length <strong>exactly</strong> <span class="math-container">$k$</span> is NP-hard on undirected graphs for all fixed <span class="math-container">$k \geq 3$</span>, see the <a href="https://scholar.archive.org/work/ky6zjna6efhybfrrg6dkfed4we/access/wayback/http://www.cs.bris.ac.uk/%7Eian/graphs/part.pdf" rel="nofollow noreferrer">paper</a> by Ian Holyer, &quot;The NP-Completeness of Some Edge-Partition Problems&quot;, SIAM J. Comput., 1981</li>
</ul>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Partial word completions with a factor compatible with another partial word</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="automata-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="counting-complexity" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="string-matching" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="string-search" />
        <author>
            <name>Antoine Amarilli 'a3nm'</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/4795</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/57039/partial-word-completions-with-a-factor-compatible-with-another-partial-word" />
        <published>2026-03-17T10:14:12Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-22T13:36:40Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Consider the alphabet <span class="math-container">$\Sigma = \{0,1\}$</span> and words over <span class="math-container">$\Sigma$</span>. A <em>partial word</em> is a word over the alphabet <span class="math-container">$\Sigma' = \{0, 1, ?\}$</span>, i.e., a word with &quot;holes&quot; that can correspond to either 0 or 1. Given a partial word <span class="math-container">$u$</span>, a <em>completion</em> of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> is a word <span class="math-container">$u'$</span> over <span class="math-container">$\Sigma$</span> obtained by filling in the holes of <span class="math-container">$u$</span>, i.e., a word such that <span class="math-container">$u'[i] = u[i]$</span> whenever <span class="math-container">$u[i] \in \Sigma$</span>. A word <span class="math-container">$u'$</span> over <span class="math-container">$\Sigma$</span> <em>matches</em> a partial word <span class="math-container">$v$</span> if some completion of <span class="math-container">$v$</span> occurs as a factor (i.e., a contiguous subword) of <span class="math-container">$u'$</span>. In other words, <span class="math-container">$v$</span> can be matched as some contiguous subword of <span class="math-container">$u'$</span> with the &quot;<span class="math-container">$?$</span>&quot;s being matched to either <span class="math-container">$0$</span> or <span class="math-container">$1$</span>.</p>
<p>I am interested in problems where I am given two partial words <span class="math-container">$u$</span> (the data) and <span class="math-container">$v$</span> (the pattern) and must answer a question about the completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that match <span class="math-container">$v$</span>. More specifically:</p>
<ul>
<li>The <strong>existential problem: is there a completion of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that matches <span class="math-container">$v$</span>?</strong>  This is sometimes called the <em>pattern matching problem with wildcards</em> (or with don't cares).</li>
<li>The <strong>universal problem: is there a completion of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that does not match <span class="math-container">$v$</span>?</strong> Equivalently, up to negation, do all completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> match <span class="math-container">$v$</span>? (Beware that this is not the same as asking whether there is some fixed completion <span class="math-container">$v'$</span> of <span class="math-container">$v$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$v'$</span> occurs in no completion of <span class="math-container">$u$</span>. In the universal problem we ask whether these is a completion of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> in which none of the completions of <span class="math-container">$v$</span> occur.)</li>
<li>The <strong>counting problem: how many completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> match <span class="math-container">$v$</span>?</strong> Note that counting the completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that do not match <span class="math-container">$v$</span> is equivalent, because these two quantities sum to <span class="math-container">$2^K$</span> for <span class="math-container">$K$</span> the number of &quot;<span class="math-container">$?$</span>&quot;s in <span class="math-container">$u$</span>.</li>
</ul>
<p>The existential problem is easily seen to be solvable in PTIME, by checking if there is an offset of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> compatible with <span class="math-container">$v$</span>. More precisely, we can use the naive algorithm checking whether there is some <span class="math-container">$j$</span> such that, for each <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i \leq |v|$</span>, the two letters <span class="math-container">$u[j+i]$</span> and <span class="math-container">$v[i]$</span> are equal or one of them is &quot;<span class="math-container">$?$</span>&quot;. Note that this can be done more efficiently using FFT, see for instance <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S002001900600250X" rel="noreferrer">Clifford and Clifford, 2007</a> -- I am not sure whether there are more efficient combinatorial algorithms.</p>
<p>However, whether the two other problems are in PTIME doesn't seem obvious. Hence my question:</p>
<p><strong>Is the universal problem above solvable in PTIME, or is it NP-hard?</strong> (or coNP-hard for the equivalent formulation) <strong>Is the counting problem above solvable in PTIME, or is it #P-hard?</strong></p>
<p>What I know so far:</p>
<ul>
<li>If the pattern is not a single partial word <span class="math-container">$v$</span> but a disjunction of partial words then the existential problem is still in PTIME but the FFT approaches do not seem to generalize (and indeed this time there is a rectangular fine-grained lower bound assuming SETH, like in the work of <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.07070" rel="noreferrer">Backurs and Indyk, 2016</a>). However, the universal and counting problems with a disjunction of partial words as the pattern are easily seen to be intractable, respectively by reduction from DNF FALSIFIABILITY or DNF #SAT. Namely, given a disjunctive normal form formula (DNF) <span class="math-container">$\Phi$</span> on <span class="math-container">$n$</span> variables with <span class="math-container">$m$</span> terms, we can translate it to a disjunction of <span class="math-container">$m$</span> partial words <span class="math-container">$v_1, \ldots, v_m$</span> where <span class="math-container">$v_i$</span> accepts the words of length <span class="math-container">$n$</span> corresponding to a Boolean valuation making the <span class="math-container">$i$</span>-th term of <span class="math-container">$\Phi$</span> true, i.e., with <span class="math-container">$0$</span> and <span class="math-container">$1$</span> at the positions of variables that occur in that term depending on the polarity of the literal and &quot;<span class="math-container">$?$</span>&quot; otherwise. Then take <span class="math-container">$u$</span> to be a partial word of length <span class="math-container">$n$</span> consisting only of &quot;<span class="math-container">$?$</span>&quot;s. There is a valuation of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that does not match <span class="math-container">$v$</span> iff <span class="math-container">$\Phi$</span> has a falsifying assignment (which is NP-hard to determine), and the number of such valuations is <span class="math-container">$2^n$</span> minus the number of satisfying assignments of <span class="math-container">$\Phi$</span> (which are #P-hard to count)</li>
<li>In the case where <span class="math-container">$u$</span> is not a partial word but a word over <span class="math-container">$\Sigma$</span>, then of course all problems are in PTIME (and the counting problem reduces to the two other problems).</li>
<li>If the notion of matching was &quot;look at the completions of the entire word <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that are compatible with the partial word <span class="math-container">$v$</span>&quot; (i.e., not &quot;have a factor compatible with <span class="math-container">$v$</span>&quot;), then all problems are clearly in PTIME (by partitioning the non-matching completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> based on the first character where there is a mismatch). For factors however these approaches don't seem to generalize (there are multiple possible offsets, and correlations across these offsets).</li>
<li><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022000012000918" rel="noreferrer">This 2013 article by Manea and Tisaneu</a> looks at problems that are very close to the counting problem above, in particular Problem 7 and Theorem 6. However their problem is about counting valuations of a word <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that are compatible with some factor of <span class="math-container">$v$</span>, not counting the valuations where some factor is compatible with <span class="math-container">$v$</span>.</li>
<li>One way to show tractability of the universal and counting problems would be to show that the language of words that don't have a factor compatible with a partial word <span class="math-container">$v$</span> can be efficiently translated (i.e., polynomially in <span class="math-container">$v$</span>) to a deterministic automaton or (for the counting problem) to an unambiguous automaton. But I don't know whether this is possible, or whether there is a lower bound on the size of such automaton representations (which would help rule out this specific approach).</li>
<li>We can solve the counting problem for approximate counting by building a nondeterministic automaton <span class="math-container">$A$</span> for the words that are completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> and match <span class="math-container">$v$</span> (by taking the union over all possible offsets) and then using an FPRAS to count the number of distinct words of length <span class="math-container">$|u|$</span> accepted by <span class="math-container">$A$</span>, see <a href="https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3477045" rel="noreferrer">Arenas et al., 2021</a>. Note that this is not the same task as multiplicatively approximating the number of completions of <span class="math-container">$u$</span> that do not match <span class="math-container">$v$</span>; I am also not sure whether there is an FPRAS for that.</li>
</ul>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Min-difference boolean convolution-like operation</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="reference-request" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="fine-grained" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="convolution" />
        <author>
            <name>alsips-cl</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/69837</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/55807/min-difference-boolean-convolution-like-operation" />
        <published>2025-10-23T13:29:47Z</published>
        <updated>2026-09-20T21:12:32Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Given two (<span class="math-container">$0$</span>-indexed) binary arrays <span class="math-container">$A$</span> and <span class="math-container">$B$</span> of size <span class="math-container">$n$</span>, I want to compute a third array <span class="math-container">$C$</span> of size <span class="math-container">$2n$</span> defined as
<span class="math-container">$$
C[k] = \min\{i-j\mid i+j=k \text{  and  } A[i] = B[j] = 1\}
$$</span>
And if there are no such values of <span class="math-container">$i, j$</span> then <span class="math-container">$C[k] = +\infty$</span> (notated as <span class="math-container">$\bullet$</span> below).</p>
<p>Example: let <span class="math-container">$A = [0, 1, 0, 1, 1]$</span> and <span class="math-container">$B = [1, 0, 1, 0, 0]$</span>, then <span class="math-container">$C = [\bullet, 1,\bullet, -1, 4, 1, 2, \bullet, \bullet]$</span>.</p>
<p>We can easily compute this in quadratic time with a double-for. Is there an <span class="math-container">$O(n^{2-\epsilon})$</span> algorithm for some <span class="math-container">$\epsilon &gt; 0$</span>? or is this false under some reasonable conjecture?</p>
<p><strong>Observation</strong>: There is a reduction to <span class="math-container">$(\min,+)$</span>-convolution, for which there is an <span class="math-container">$n^2/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log n})}$</span> algorithm (<a href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/10237/does-the-convolution-theorem-apply-to-weaker-algebraic-structures">link</a>). The reduction goes: define arrays <span class="math-container">$A'$</span> and <span class="math-container">$B'$</span> by
<span class="math-container">$$
A'[i] = \begin{cases}
i &amp;\text{ if } A[i] = 1\\
+\infty&amp;\text{ if } A[i] = 0\\
\end{cases}
$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$
B'[i] = \begin{cases}
-i &amp;\text{ if } B[i] = 1\\
+\infty&amp;\text{ if } B[i] = 0\\
\end{cases}
$$</span>
Feeding these arrays to a <span class="math-container">$(\min,+)$</span>-convolution gives the target <span class="math-container">$C$</span>.</p>
<p>It has been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3293465" rel="nofollow noreferrer">conjectured</a> that there is no <span class="math-container">$O(n^{2-\epsilon})$</span> algorithm for <span class="math-container">$(\min,+)$</span>-convolution; indeed, a reduction the other way would answer my question, but it doesn't seem likely.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Complexity of word matrix realizability problem</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="cc.complexity-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="fl.formal-languages" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="matrices" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="permutations" />
        <author>
            <name>Antoine Amarilli 'a3nm'</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/4795</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/55797/complexity-of-word-matrix-realizability-problem" />
        <published>2025-10-14T16:18:52Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-21T16:07:16Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$\Sigma$</span> be an alphabet of cardinality <span class="math-container">$\geq 2$</span>. For <span class="math-container">$d$</span> an integer, a <em><span class="math-container">$d$</span>-word-matrix</em> is a square matrix <span class="math-container">$M$</span> with <span class="math-container">$d$</span> rows and <span class="math-container">$d$</span> columns where each cell contains a word: formally, for each <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i,j \leq d$</span> the matrix contains a word <span class="math-container">$M[i,j]$</span>.</p>
<p>Given a <span class="math-container">$d$</span>-word-matrix, for <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i \leq d$</span> we define its <em><span class="math-container">$i$</span>-th row word</em> <span class="math-container">$M[i,\bullet]$</span> as the concatenation of the words of the <span class="math-container">$i$</span>-th row in order, formally <span class="math-container">$M[i,\bullet] := M[i,1] \cdots M[i,d]$</span>, and the <em><span class="math-container">$i$</span>-th column word</em> <span class="math-container">$M[\bullet,i]$</span> as the concatenation of the words of the <span class="math-container">$i$</span>-th column in order, formally <span class="math-container">$M[\bullet,i] := M[1,i] \cdots M[d,i]$</span>. Then the <em>row concatenation</em> of <span class="math-container">$M$</span> is the concatenation <span class="math-container">$R(M) := M[1,\bullet] \cdots M[d,\bullet]$</span> of the row words in order, and the <em>column concatenation</em> of <span class="math-container">$M$</span> is the concatenation <span class="math-container">$C(M) := M[\bullet,1] \cdots M[\bullet,d]$</span> of the column words in order.</p>
<p>For instance the following is a 3-word-matrix whose row concatenation is <span class="math-container">$ababbba$</span> and whose column concatenation is <span class="math-container">$abbbbaa$</span>:
<span class="math-container">\begin{bmatrix}
ab &amp; \epsilon &amp; a \\
b &amp; \epsilon &amp; \epsilon \\
\epsilon &amp; bb &amp; a
\end{bmatrix}</span></p>
<p>I am interested in the following <em>word matrix realizability problem</em>. We are given as input two words <span class="math-container">$r,c \in \Sigma^*$</span> and an integer <span class="math-container">$d$</span>. Our goal is to decide whether there exists a <span class="math-container">$d$</span>-word matrix <span class="math-container">$M$</span> with <span class="math-container">$R(M) = r$</span> and <span class="math-container">$C(M) = c$</span>. <strong>Is this problem in PTIME, or is it NP-hard?</strong></p>
<p>Some preliminary observations:</p>
<ul>
<li>First, the answer can only be true if the words <span class="math-container">$r$</span> and <span class="math-container">$c$</span> have the same length, and more precisely they must have the same <em>Parikh image</em>, i.e., every letter must occur as many times in <span class="math-container">$r$</span> and in <span class="math-container">$c$</span>.</li>
<li>For <span class="math-container">$d=1$</span>, the answer is yes precisely when <span class="math-container">$r=c$</span>.</li>
<li>For <span class="math-container">$d=2$</span> the problem asks whether we can transform <span class="math-container">$r$</span> into <span class="math-container">$c$</span> by one internal swap, i.e., if there is a decomposition <span class="math-container">$r = s t u v$</span> such that we also have <span class="math-container">$s u t v = c$</span>. It can be solved in PTIME by bruteforcing the possible decompositions <span class="math-container">$r = s t u v$</span> (of which there are <span class="math-container">$O(|r|^3)$</span>) and checking whether they satisfy the other requirement. (I'm not sure of what is the best possible exponent for the case <span class="math-container">$d=2$</span>.)</li>
<li>More generally, for any fixed value of <span class="math-container">$d$</span>, the problem is in PTIME by bruteforcing the <span class="math-container">$d^2-1$</span> possible choices of cut points in <span class="math-container">$r$</span>, but of course this approach does not generalize when <span class="math-container">$d$</span> is given as input.</li>
<li>One can also check that for large enough <span class="math-container">$d$</span> relative to <span class="math-container">$r$</span> and <span class="math-container">$c$</span> (i.e., <span class="math-container">$d \geq |r|$</span>) the answer is always yes provided that <span class="math-container">$r$</span> and <span class="math-container">$c$</span> have same Parikh image. Indeed, the condition on the Parikh image ensures that we can define a bijection <span class="math-container">$\pi$</span> on <span class="math-container">$\{1,\ldots,|r|\}$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$r_i = c_{\pi(i)}$</span> for each <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i \leq |r|$</span>. Now we can define <span class="math-container">$M$</span> so that <span class="math-container">$M[i,\pi(i)]$</span> contains the single-letter word <span class="math-container">$r_i$</span> for each <span class="math-container">$1 \leq i \leq |r|$</span> and all other cells are empty, i.e., contain the empty word <span class="math-container">$\epsilon$</span>. Then by construction we have <span class="math-container">$R(M) = r$</span> and it can be checked that <span class="math-container">$C(M) = r_{\pi^{-1}(1)} \cdots r_{\pi^{-1}(|r|)} = c$</span>.</li>
</ul>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">Show that the first agent weakly prefers their own bundle to anybody else's</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="ds.algorithms" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="gt.game-theory" />
        <author>
            <name>breakfasttheorist</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/75487</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/55417/show-that-the-first-agent-weakly-prefers-their-own-bundle-to-anybody-elses" />
        <published>2025-05-21T15:12:28Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-21T16:05:55Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Suppose we have a set <span class="math-container">$N$</span> of <span class="math-container">$n$</span> players and a set <span class="math-container">$M$</span> of <span class="math-container">$m$</span> items. We are given a matrix <span class="math-container">$P_{n \times m}$</span> whose element <span class="math-container">$p_{ij} \geq 0$</span> <span class="math-container">$(i \in N, m \in M)$</span> denotes the valuation of good <span class="math-container">$j$</span> by player <span class="math-container">$i$</span>. Let <span class="math-container">$v = [v_1, v_2, \cdots, v_n]$</span> be a vector of valuation functions defined as <span class="math-container">$v_i(S) = \sum_{j \in S} p_{ij}$</span> for all <span class="math-container">$S \subseteq M$</span> and <span class="math-container">$i \in N$</span>. We additionally have <span class="math-container">$v_i(\{\}) = 0$</span> for all <span class="math-container">$i \in N$</span>.</p>
<p><strong>Introduce an additional constraint:</strong> Each agent values each bundle uniquely. That is, for any agent <span class="math-container">$i \in N$</span> and any two bundles <span class="math-container">$S, S' \subseteq M$</span>, <span class="math-container">$[v_i(S) = v_i(S') \iff S = S']$</span>.</p>
<p>Consider a distribution protocol or the order in which the objects will be picked up by a player:</p>
<pre><code>Number players from 1 through n
While there are unclaimed objects:
    Let each player from 1 through n claim one unclaimed item one-by-one
</code></pre>
<p>Put simply, players take turns picking items in sequence from the first to the <span class="math-container">$n^{\text{th}}$</span> player, repeating the cycle until all items are chosen.</p>
<p><strong>Game Description:</strong> Consider a perfect-information sequential game that follows the distribution protocol described above. That is, the game starts with the first player choosing from a set of <span class="math-container">$m$</span> items. After that, the second player picks an item from the remaining <span class="math-container">$m - 1$</span> items, then the third from <span class="math-container">$m - 2$</span>, and so on, until the <span class="math-container">$n$</span>th player chooses one from what's left. Once all <span class="math-container">$n$</span> players have taken a turn, the game loops back to the first player, who now chooses one from <span class="math-container">$m - n$</span> items. This picking order continues in rounds until all items are allocated.</p>
<p>Along any path or in any sub-game, <strong>the utility of player <span class="math-container">$i$</span></strong> is given by the valuation <span class="math-container">$v_i$</span> of the allocation he gets.</p>
<p><strong>Example:</strong> Consider the following game with <span class="math-container">$2$</span> players and <span class="math-container">$4$</span> items.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>The SPNE paths are marked in red. As such, we assume sequential rationality and employ a backward induction method to find these paths.</p>
</li>
<li><p>Payoffs: The utility of player <span class="math-container">$i$</span>, when employing strategy <span class="math-container">$s_i$</span>, is given by <span class="math-container">$v_i(A_{(s_i, s_{-i})})$</span>, where <span class="math-container">$A_{(s_i, s_{-i})}$</span> denotes the allocation resulting from player <span class="math-container">$i$</span> choosing strategy <span class="math-container">$s_i$</span> and the remaining players following strategies <span class="math-container">$s_{-i}$</span>.</p>
<p>Look at the second SPNE path: <span class="math-container">$c \to b \to a$</span>. Here, <span class="math-container">$1$</span> gets <span class="math-container">$\{a,c\}$</span> and <span class="math-container">$2$</span> gets <span class="math-container">$\{b\}$</span> and so the utility vector is <span class="math-container">$[v1(\{a,c\}, v_2(\{b\}))] = [6,5]$</span>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://i.sstatic.net/WihYlXrw.png" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/WihYlXrw.png" alt="enter image description here" /></a></p>
<p><strong>Question:</strong> <strong>Show (or disprove) that if an arbitrary <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgame_perfect_equilibrium" rel="nofollow noreferrer">Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium</a> outcome results in allocations <span class="math-container">$(A_1^*, A_2^*, \cdots, A_n^*)$</span>, then it must be that for all <span class="math-container">$j \in N$</span>, <span class="math-container">$v_1(A_1^{*}) \geq v_1(A_j^{*})]$</span>.</strong> In simpler terms, show that in <em>every</em> SPNE outcome, the first agent weakly prefers their own bundle to anyone else's.</p>
<p>Only the case for two agents (and arbitrary number of goods) has been solved so far. The general case remains open. <a href="https://cs.stackexchange.com/a/171847/181227">Click on this link</a> for the solution. Moreover, excluding the &quot;additional constraint&quot; gives us counterexamples as discussed <a href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/a/55396/75487">here</a>.</p>
<p>(Note: Problems similar to this have been posted on this site and cs.stackexchange before. However, this one is a completely new variant of the same problem.)</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">What is the smallest graph of treewidth $k$ having less edges than the $(k+1)$-clique?</title>
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="graph-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="treewidth" />
            <category scheme="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/tags" term="extremal-combinatorics" />
        <author>
            <name>Antoine Amarilli 'a3nm'</name>
            <uri>https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/users/4795</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/53806/what-is-the-smallest-graph-of-treewidth-k-having-less-edges-than-the-k1-c" />
        <published>2024-01-24T10:36:19Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T15:43:52Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treewidth" rel="noreferrer">Treewidth</a> is a graph parameter measuring how close a graph is to being a tree. I am interested in what is the minimal number of edges required for a graph to have treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span>.</p>
<p>A natural family of graphs to consider are the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clique_(graph_theory)" rel="noreferrer">cliques</a>: a clique on <span class="math-container">$k+1$</span> vertices has treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span>, and has <span class="math-container">$k (k+1) / 2$</span> edges. However, asymptotically, there are graphs of treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span> whose number of edges is linear rather than quadratic, e.g., cubic expanders as mentioned in <a href="https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/39071/maximum-treewidth-of-a-graphs-with-m-edges">this question</a>. So cliques are not optimal. My question is: <strong>what is the smallest example of a graph of treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span> having less edges than the <span class="math-container">$(k+1)$</span>-clique?</strong></p>
<p>I have checked experimentally that all graphs of 14 edges or less have treewidth at most 4, so they do not beat the 6-clique which has 15 edges and treewidth 5. Hence, the smallest treewidth for which I do not know the answer is 6. Specifically: the 7-clique has 21 edges and treewidth 6, but <strong>is there a graph of treewidth 6 having 20 edges or less?</strong></p>
<p>(Note that we could ask the same question of the minimal number of <em>vertices</em> required for a graph to have treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span>, but then it is uninteresting: you need <span class="math-container">$k+1$</span> vertices for a graph to have treewidth <span class="math-container">$k$</span>, and this is achieved by the <span class="math-container">$(k+1)$</span>-clique.)</p>

        </summary>
